MOTOR FREIGHT COMES TO CARVELL FALLS
A truck depot opens at the works; ore from the far patches by road

The company has opened a truck depot. Goods that arrive by belt wait in its yard for a truck; a truck runs between two depots and what it brings leaves by belt again. The Courier notes that roads are cheap and trucks are not.
Station built; trains to run point to point, one to a block

A rail station stands at the works. Trains carry more than any truck and run between two stations. Only one train may hold a stretch of track between signals, so the company will want signals as the line grows.
A landing on the bank; river freight is the cheapest ton the company moves
The company has built a barge landing on the river. Barges are slow and carry a great deal; they run between two landings and go wherever the water goes.

NEW WORKS TO RISE ON CARVELL RIVER
Young firm takes ground beside the iron seam; townsfolk expect smoke by spring

CARVELL FALLS — A new concern has taken the flats east of town, where the ground is thick with iron ore. The company has {0}, a line of credit at the bank, and not one building to its name.

The Courier's advice: look about first. Hold the middle mouse button or the W, A, S and D keys to move the eye over the ground, and turn the wheel to draw near or stand back. The stippled patch is the iron seam.

Then buy a MINE HEAD from the classified advertisements (Tab opens this paper; the advertisement is ringed in red) and set it down on the seam. The more seams under its four feet, the faster it raises ore. Press R to turn it so its chute faces where the belts will go.
FIRST ORE HAULED — WHERE TO NEXT?
Mine head raises its first tons; ore piles up with nowhere to go

The new mine head is up and turning, and iron ore is coming out of its chute by the ton. Ore in a heap is worth nothing, so the next purchase is belting.

CANVAS BELTING is five dollars the yard. Pick it from the classifieds, click at the chute and drag a run across the ground; turn corners as you go. Every mine, mill and shop fires on coal: each comes with a bag of thirty lumps in its firebox, which is plenty to begin with. A coal seam lies to the west; give each building a belt of its own for coal, on another side from its ore. Never mix coal into an ore line: a full firebox refuses the lump, and the whole belt stops behind it.

Run the ore to a SMELTER, ringed in red. Ore in on any side; iron ingots out of the chute.
IRON FROM CARVELL FALLS HITS MARKET
First ingot poured; freight agents ask when the goods will ship

The smelter has poured its first iron ingot, and the ingots are stacking up. A FREIGHT DEPOT, ringed in red, buys anything belted into it at the day's price, and the money is in the till at once.\n\nThe day's prices are printed on the MARKET page of this paper. Every good has a selling price and a buying price, and both move: with the trade of the nation, with the events of the day, and with what you yourself have lately sold.
Buyers grow tired of one thing; the price of iron sags under the flood

The freight agents report that iron from Carvell Falls is piling up in the yards, and the price paid for it has fallen. Sell a great deal of any one good and its price sinks; leave it alone and the price climbs back over a day or two.\n\nThe remedy is variety. A PRESS, ringed in red, flattens ingots into IRON PLATE, which fetches more and sells to a fresh set of buyers. Split the ingot line and feed some to a press. Later, the same trick with steel, wire and castings will carry the works up to motorcars.
BANKER EXTENDS CREDIT TO YOUNG FIRM
The Carvell Falls Savings Bank opens a line of {0} to the young firm

Now that the works is trading, the bank has opened a line of credit to it. The masthead shows it: CASH on hand, CREDIT drawn against the limit, and the SHARE price, which is the score of the game.

Any purchase beyond your cash draws on the line without a word. Cash in the till repays it each night. Every week the bank charges interest on the balance; the rate is printed on the market page.

Mind this: if one week the interest cannot be met from cash and what remains of the line, the bank forecloses and the company is finished. The Courier runs a BANKER'S WARNING a week ahead whenever that is in prospect. Do not ignore it.
Out-of-town firm wires an order; the works is known beyond the county

The first telegram has come over the wire: a firm wants iron plate, a set quantity by a set day. Orders are printed on the TELEGRAM DESK page. They are filled by selling the good through any depot before the day named; the price is the market's, the reward is the headline, and a missed order makes a headline of another kind.

To keep several lines fed, a SPLITTER, ringed in red, takes goods from either side and deals them out even-handed to two belts. A SORTING SPLITTER sends one kind of good left and everything else right: pick the good off a belt with Q and click the splitter to set it.

Stand back with the wheel and the belts turn to flow lines, heavier as they fill, and red where they are backed up. Press F for the flow overlay: goods a minute on every line, what each idle machine wants, and FIRE OUT wherever a firebox has gone cold.
The depot has taken its first delivery of iron from the works. Money in the till.
FIRST STEEL POURED IN CARVELL FALLS
Open hearth tapped; the town looks for beams, rods and wire to follow

The open-hearth furnace at the works was tapped this morning and the first steel ingot rolled out onto the belts. Iron, coke and limestone go in; steel comes out, and from steel comes nearly everything else the catalog sells: plate for the press, rod and wire from the drawing mill, beams from the rolling mill.
Engine, chassis and body married on the assembly line; crowd gathers at the gate
An automobile built entirely at Carvell Falls left the final assembly line today under its own power. It is the first of what the company hopes will be many.
The thousandth motorcar leaves the works
The works has built its thousandth automobile. Dealers from three states are on the telephone.
FIRST MOTOR TRUCK LEAVES THE LINE
Same engine and chassis as the motorcar, a flat bed where the body would go
The final assembly line turned out a motor truck today. The company says it will haul the works' own goods once the roads are laid; until then it waits in the yard with a price on it.
Hangar doors open; machine circles the town and lands to cheers
The first aeroplane assembled at the works flew this afternoon. The Courier's reporter counted four circuits of the town.
A waterwheel has been set on the bank. Whatever stands beside it runs on the river and burns no coal.
Boiler lit; pipes to carry power where belts of coal once ran
The first boiler was lit today. Steam in pipes reaches every machine on the line and gets twice the work from a lump of coal.
Power station hums; poles march across the works
Current flows. Machines within reach of a pole run a quarter faster, and the electric shops can at last be set to work.
DAM COMPLETED — VALLEY FLOODS AS PLANNED

The dam across the Carvell is closed and the valley above it is filling. Power without fuel, for as long as the river runs.

The company could not meet its weekly interest and the bank has foreclosed. The works stands silent. This is the last edition the Courier will print for it; the archive remains.
